entities.name: Tamás Bakócz
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tamás Bakócz (1442, Ardud – June 25, 1521), a towering figure in early 16th-century Hungarian and Papal politics, ascended from humble serf origins to become Archbishop of Esztergom, Cardinal, and a serious contender for the papacy. His remarkable career spanned the reigns of Hungarian kings Matthias Corvinus and Vladislaus II Jagiellon, during a period when the Kingdom of Hungary faced increasing Ottoman pressure and internal aristocratic struggles. Bakócz leveraged his exceptional administrative acumen, legal training, and diplomatic skill to accumulate immense power and wealth, becoming one of the wealthiest and most influential prelates in Europe, deeply entwined with both secular governance and ecclesiastical authority.

As Chancellor of Hungary from 1490, Bakócz effectively governed the kingdom for King Vladislaus II, navigating the complex political landscape through a blend of shrewd alliances and financial manipulation. His influence reached its zenith following his elevation to cardinal by Pope Alexander VI in 1500 and his subsequent appointment as Patriarch of Constantinople in 1507. In 1513, after the death of Pope Julius II, Bakócz traveled to Rome and actively campaigned for the papal throne in the conclave, coming remarkably close to election before Leo X ultimately secured the papacy. His ambition was further demonstrated when, in 1514, Pope Leo X granted him a papal bull to preach a crusade against the Ottoman Empire, appointing him its legate.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tamás Bakócz significantly shaped Hungarian politics for over three decades, rising to become one of the most powerful figures in the kingdom and nearly becoming Pope. His actions, particularly the call for a crusade, directly triggered the Dózsa Peasant Revolt, a pivotal event in Hungarian social history with long-lasting consequences for serfdom.
